Read only the supplied manuscript images. Do not search for the text, open a
catalogue or edition, or consult an earlier transcription. Do not identify the
work or author. If prior context has already revealed a proposed identification
or reading, stop and report that exposure instead of calling this a blind reading.

Begin with a brief image-only layout survey. Note orientation, columns, running
titles, rubrics, enlarged initials, underlined text, and interlinear or marginal
glosses when visible. Distinguish observations from tentative interpretations
such as main text with commentary. Do not infer author, work, date, or provenance.
A tight crop may not show the layout; say so rather than guessing.

Use those features to choose a few useful spans: headings or question openings,
then connecting prose, transitions or citation chains. Keep quoted lemmata and
commentary separate. Read enough surrounding prose to make a later source match
checkable; a full transcription is not required. State which areas you selected
and which remain unread. Suggest a wider view or an adjacent crop if needed.

Transcribe those spans, preserving physical lines. Label each line with its
image filename and a line number counted from the top of that image. Keep columns
and marginal additions separate. Note overlapping crops rather than treating
repeated lines as additional text.

Retain abbreviation marks when possible. Put proposed expansions in parentheses,
uncertain readings before a question mark, and unreadable text in [illegible].
Describe visible deletions and additions explicitly. Do not supply missing words
from what would make grammatical or philosophical sense. Leave uncertainty visible.

Return the reading as UTF-8 plain text. Include limitations (cropped lines, damage,
uncertain column order) in that same response. This is an unverified image reading.

text:
packet-18 - unverified image reading (first reader)
No prior identification or reading of this record was visible in my context before reading.

LAYOUT SURVEY

image-001.jpg (reduced overview, photographed on black ground with colour checker and ruler at right edge):
Several separate pieces of parchment laid out together, some in plastic sleeves, with grey redaction boxes over modern labels.
 - Upper left: a small piece (label/spine-title?) written in a later, careful hand in brownish ink: "Biblia sacra / cum / Explicatione / nom[...] [oval stamp/number "17"] [...]hebr." with "1514" below and a pencil shelfmark "Stams, STA, Fig. 168-3r?" partly under the grey box. Observation: looks like a book label written on a reused piece. Not main text.
 - Middle left: a wider piece with large textualis letters showing only in mirror image (offset/show-through), pencil "Stams, STA, Fig. 168-4r?" top right. Two lines of large script visible reversed.
 - Small scrap below it in its own sleeve, with a red mark.
 - Upper right: a damaged piece (two parts, torn, with clear tape/sleeve) with red-and-black calendar-type entries: large red initials and red date words ("[..]Idus", "[..]kl"), followed by black entries in a later cursive/semi-cursive hand ("Obiit venerabilis ... Monachus ... Sacerdos ..."), red marginal word "Missa" with cross signs. Pencil "Stams, STA, Fig. 168-1r". Tentative: an obituary/necrology-type calendar with entries in several hands.
 - Lower right: a ruled piece, largely blank or very faded, with ruled frame lines, stains; pencil "Stams, STA, Fig. 168-2r".

image-002.jpg (native tile of the upper-left label piece, "168-3r?"):
Later hand (humanistic/early modern book hand), brown ink, large letters. Not medieval main text; reads as a title label:
002.1  Biblia Sacra
002.2  cum:
002.3  Explicatione
002.4  nom[...] [oval paper label with "17." pasted over] [..]i? hebr.   (probably "nom(inum) ... hebr(aicorum)"? - the middle is hidden by the pasted label; expansion is a guess)
002.5  1514.   (below, in a different, later ink, partly on the paper label edge)
Pencil at lower left: "Stams, STA, Fig. 168-3r" (partly cut).
A vertical strip at left (about one sixth of the width) looks like a separate/overlapping strip of parchment with a faint red stroke; no text read there.

image-003.jpg (native tile of the middle-left piece, pencil "Stams, STA, Fig. 168-4r"):
The visible script is ONLY a mirror-image offset (ink transferred from a facing written surface, or show-through), not writing on this face. I made a horizontally flipped copy, crop-003-flip.jpg, to read it.
Two lines of very large textualis (formata), letter height c. 1.5 cm+ judging by the overview scale, brown offset; probably a liturgical book with large script (choirbook/antiphoner-size). Reading of the flipped image:
003.1  D?ominu[.] [n/u]...[..]num    (first letter a large rounded D or O; "Dominu..." is possible but uncertain; middle obscured by a darker horizontal blot with strokes)
003.2  [..]in ea? Ma?g[...]num?    (minims dominate; I can only say "in" and possibly "ea" then a capital-like M/A)
Very uncertain; the offset is blurred and minims cannot be counted reliably. No other text on this face.

image-004.jpg (small scrap in its own sleeve): no script; a single red stroke (part of a red initial or rubric line?) only. Nothing to transcribe.

image-005.jpg (native tile, upper part of the upper-right piece, pencil 168-1r on overview):
Layout observations: ruled in drypoint/plummet with horizontal lines and vertical bounding lines; a narrow column at left (letter column?) then the entry field. Calendar-type: red date word with a large red decorated initial (cadel-style penwork I/T), then black entries in a 16th-century(?) German-style cursive with Latin; red strokes touch some capitals (rubricated capital strokes). A tear runs diagonally through the middle, mended with clear film. Upper right margin, later hand, black: "Januarius".
Lines counted from top of the image:
005.1  (top right margin)  Januari[us]
005.2  f [large red cadel initial I] Idus   Obiit venerabilis [?]e? fr[ater?] ...    ("f" in black in the left letter column = calendar letter; "Idus" red; "Obiit" read from O-bu-it with a red-touched capital O/D: "Obiit" is likely but the 'ii' are compressed; "venerabilis" abbreviated "venerab[i]l[is]")
